segments.text: It's 1902 in French Indochina, and colonial authorities are pouring money into making
Hanoi look like a European capital.
They are paving wide, elegant avenues and constructing massive administrative buildings
like the Banque Franco-Chinoise.
To support all this modern surface infrastructure, engineers installed a sprawling, state-of-the-art
underground sewer system across the city.
But those dark, predator-free tunnels provided a perfect environment.
– almost immediately they became a protected superhighway for an exploding, chaotic swarm
of rats.
So while residents enjoyed the calm, orderly street-level view of rickshaws rolling past
the city gates, directly beneath their feet, a massive biological threat was multiplying
rapidly.
The colonial authorities had inadvertently built a parallel world – an underground
city that turned their symbol of modern hygiene into an invisible, protected sanctuary
for disease.
To eliminate the pests quickly, the colonial administration launched a highly scalable
bounty program.
They offered citizens exactly one cent for every dead rat.
They needed a way to track the kills without handling thousands of diseased carcasses.
As this diagram shows, the transaction was simple.
A citizen hands over a tail, and the government hands over a coin.
Immediately, tails poured into collection centers by thousands.
submissions, the daily submissions chart spiked upward in a vertical line. Inside the
colonial offices, administrators celebrated. They looked at the soaring submission numbers
and concluded that their population was fully engaged and the rat threat was days
away from being wiped out. When leaders fixate on a single data point, high engagement
looks exactly like success. The metric creates a protective illusion that blinds them
to the actual reality on the ground. Then, city officials and local police started
noticing something very strange.
The streets were suddenly full of completely healthy, active
rats scurrying around without any tails.
The rat hunters had done the math
and realized a basic biological loophole.
A rat does not actually need its tail to live a full life
and more importantly, it doesn't need a tail
to keep having babies.
Instead of doing the hard work of pest extermination,
citizens shifted to harvesting.
They simply snipped off the valuable part
and let the animal escape back into the sewers.
The hunters were acting as rational economic actors.
They recognized a reliable income stream and made the logical choice to preserve the resource
that provided it.
Any time you establish a strict financial boundary or rule, humans will study it and
figure out how to extract the maximum possible payout while doing the absolute minimum
amount of work.
The hustle soon evolved from opportunistic snips in the alleys into a highly organized
systemic exploitation by the local trade economy.
A few particularly entrepreneurial citizens realized they didn't even need to hunt
in the sewers at all. They began quietly setting up dedicated, mass-scale rat breeding
farms. Here is the operational logic of a rat farm. You take two surviving, tailless
rats, let them breed, and harvest the offspring. It turns a one-time bounty into a self-sustaining,
limitless machine that prints coins. These mass breeding operations scaled up
rapidly across the outskirts of the city, generating consistent profits
entirely out of sight of the French administrators. A government program
explicitly designed to eradicate a specific pest inadvertently built the
exact market conditions needed to finance its mass production.
Eventually, health inspectors stumbled upon the breeding farms. The colonial
government panicked and immediately canceled the entire bounty program. This graphic shows
the catastrophic tally. On the left, a mountain of paid-for rat tails.
On the right, the living rat population was significantly larger than before. Economists
call this Goodhart's Law. When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good
measure. The most chilling part of the 1902 Hanoi crisis is that nobody actually
broke the rules, the hunters delivered the tales,
and the government paid the cents.
Every mechanical gear of the plan
functioned exactly as designed.
